title: George Floyd Response - 'Dominate the Streets' Military Crackdown
description_short: George Floyd Response - 'Dominate the Streets' Military Crackdown
description_medium: On June 1, 2020, President Donald Trump urged governors to deploy the National Guard in enough numbers to “dominate the streets” and said he would send the military if they did not act. In a later interview, he said many George Floyd protesters were following the crowd. These reports document his public statements, but not who ordered specific tactics during the Lafayette Square clearing.
description_long: Donald Trump's response to nationwide protests over George Floyd's killing was to threaten military deployment to 'dominate the streets' and dismiss demonstrators as people who 'just didn't know' what they were protesting, demonstrating his complete inability to understand or address racial injustice. After Floyd was killed by Minneapolis police on May 25, 2020, millions of Americans took to the streets in the largest civil rights protests in U.S. history, but Trump's focus was on using overwhelming force to suppress demonstrations rather than addressing police brutality. In a Rose Garden speech on June 1, Trump declared he would deploy 'thousands and thousands of heavily armed soldiers, military personnel and law enforcement officers' while police fired tear gas on peaceful protesters across the street. Trump recommended that governors deploy the National Guard in sufficient numbers to 'dominate the streets,' and threatened that if they failed to act, he would deploy federal military forces to 'quickly solve the problem for them.' The president showed no empathy for Floyd's death or understanding of the systemic racism that sparked the protests, instead viewing the demonstrations purely as a law enforcement challenge requiring military solutions. When asked about protesters' goals, Trump claimed many 'really weren't able to say' why they were demonstrating, dismissing the clear demands for police reform and racial justice. His militaristic response and dismissive attitude toward protesters represented a complete failure of presidential leadership during a critical moment in American racial reckoning, prioritizing authoritarian force over addressing legitimate grievances about police violence.

title: Terminates TPS for El Salvador
description_short: DHS announced termination of Temporary Protected Status for El Salvador, jeopardizing legal status for many residents.
description_medium: On January 8, 2018, DHS Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen announced that El Salvador’s Temporary Protected Status designation would end after an 18-month transition, effective September 9, 2019. DHS said recovery from the 2001 earthquakes was largely complete and the conditions supporting the designation no longer persisted. Congressional Research Service reporting estimated about 195,000 Salvadoran TPS beneficiaries would be affected.
description_long: DHS announced on January 8, 2018, that it would terminate El Salvador’s Temporary Protected Status designation, which had been granted after the country’s 2001 earthquakes. Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen said the department had reviewed country conditions and consulted other agencies; the Federal Register notice concluded that earthquake recovery was largely complete and the statutory conditions for the designation were no longer met. The notice set September 9, 2019, as the termination date, 18 months after the then-current designation ended, to allow an orderly transition. Beneficiaries could re-register and seek employment authorization through the transition period. The Congressional Research Service estimated that about 195,000 Salvadoran TPS beneficiaries were affected. This was an announced termination with a delayed effective date, not an immediate end to protection on January 8. The notice records DHS’s rationale and timeline; it does not establish that every beneficiary later lost status or was removed from the United States. The Federal Register docket also records subsequent actions on the designation, so this entry describes the 2018 decision rather than the program’s later legal status.
subcategory: Legal Immigration Status Revocation and Humanitarian Protection Elimination

title: DOJ Urges Court to Strike the ACA
description_short: The Trump Justice Department argued that the Affordable Care Act should be struck down in court.
description_medium: In June 2018, the Trump Justice Department told a federal court it would no longer defend the ACA’s individual-mandate requirement after Congress reduced its tax penalty to zero. DOJ argued the mandate was then unconstitutional and that the law’s guaranteed-issue and community-rating protections could not stand without it. The filing concerned two ACA protections in a pending Texas lawsuit, not a request to invalidate every provision of the Act.
description_long: In June 2018, the Justice Department changed its position in Texas v. United States, a pending challenge to the Affordable Care Act in federal district court. Attorney General Jeff Sessions said DOJ would not defend the constitutionality of the ACA’s minimum-coverage provision, Section 5000A(a), after the 2017 tax law set its penalty at zero beginning in 2019. The department argued that the Supreme Court’s earlier reading of the mandate as a tax would no longer apply because the provision would produce no revenue. DOJ also agreed with the plaintiffs that the mandate was inseverable from two protections for people with pre-existing conditions: guaranteed issue, which limits insurers’ ability to deny coverage, and community rating, which restricts premium discrimination. The filing did not argue that every ACA provision should be struck down. It stated the administration’s litigation position while the case was pending; it was not a court ruling. A federal district judge later accepted a broader challenge, but the Supreme Court ultimately dismissed the case in 2021 for lack of standing. The episode documents the administration’s effort to remove two core protections through litigation and the procedural distinction between a party’s argument and a final judgment.
subcategory: Social Safety Net Destruction and Vulnerable Population Abandonment
